doc.title: Frank Alkyer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 10, 2020

title: Covering many jazz styles; the 'crewcut' contest and the Maher family ownership
summary: Asked about the Mississippi Rag and balancing styles, Alkyer recalls DownBeat's contest to rename jazz and describes the family-owned business, which values editorial craft.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Okay. Are you familiar with a publication called the Mississippi Rag?
Okay. So the fellow that bought it is actually an acquaintance of mine in Utica, New York. He bought it and he changed the name to The Syncopated Times.

So the reason I brought this up, they have this niche within a niche and they are very faithful and sometimes semi-obnoxious about what this music is — which leads me to ask do you have some kind of way of keeping track of what kind of jazz you’ve written about in the last ten issues and what do you project for the next ten? Because there’s so many styles out there and some could be forgotten.

I might get the date wrong on this, but DownBeat ran a contest to re-name jazz because jazz had become — it came to mean too many things to too many people. And we offered a thousand dollars for the winner. We wrote an editorial, put it out there and had this contest. That was in 1939 I believe. And the winning entry? Was crewcut.

What the heck was that? Well okay let’s just like throw another 70 or 80 years of jazz history on top of that and you go, we can’t, no, we’re just going to go — luckily we’re still a family-owned publication. The Maher family, Kevin Maher owns it, his father owned it before him, his grandfather owned it before him. And so, and they’re not jazz people. They’re business people. And they’ve stayed — but they’ve always stayed out of the way and they’ve always had an appreciation for good editorial, that they thought they had a philosophy that good editorial will mean good ad sales because that means we’re going to have a bigger audience that’s going to want to read. So that, into this is what I was hired into and man oh man, when I talk to people at other publications and you know, going through hard times, I think that we still succeed for a few reasons. Number one jazz education, number two we’re still allowed to apply our craft and really look at it as a craft and not just content. You know everybody uses the word content. We don’t use that in our office. What we do is we craft fine articles and we craft fine design. And we work hard.
